docs.title: stoke
docs.text:
Build, run, and scaffold projects in multiple languages.

stoke unifies development workflows for Python, Java, C, C++, Go, Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, and TypeScript projects. One command-line interface for building, running, watching, and scaffolding — including popular frameworks like Spring Boot, FastAPI, Flask, Django, Gin, Express, Next.js, Actix-web, Ktor, ASP.NET Core, and more. Configure your project once in stoke.toml, and stoke handles compilation, dependency management, IDE integration, and more.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Multi-language: Build Python, Java, C, C++, Go, Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, and TypeScript projects with the same commands
  • Language installation: Install Python/JDK/gcc/Go/Node.js via stoke install
  • Framework scaffolding: Spring Boot, FastAPI, Flask, Django, plus web frameworks for Go, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, and PHP
  • Python environments: venv or conda
  • Fast: Incremental compilation with header dependency tracking
  • Simple: One stoke.toml for the whole project
  • Watch mode: Auto-rebuild on file changes
  • Hot-reload: Restart processes on rebuild
  • IDE integration: Auto-generates VSCode/Eclipse/IntelliJ configs
  • Build profiles: Debug/Release/custom profiles
  • Dependency management: pip for Python, Maven for Java, vcpkg for C/C++, go.mod for Go, Cargo for Rust, Gradle for Kotlin, NuGet for C#, Bundler for Ruby, Composer for PHP, npm for JavaScript/TypeScript

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Create stoke.toml:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["src/**/*.cpp"]

Build and run:

stoke build
stoke run

That's it.

docs.title: What is stoke?
docs.text: A build tool that unifies workflows for Python, Java, C, C++, Go, Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, and TypeScript. One stoke.toml per project, one set of commands for all languages.

docs.title: Why not use language-specific tools?
docs.text:
Language-specific tools (pip, Maven, Make, Cargo) are excellent. But when you work across multiple languages, remembering which command builds what, configuring each ecosystem separately, and coordinating IDE setups becomes friction.

stoke provides a consistent interface without replacing the underlying tools. Under the hood, stoke uses pip, javac, Maven, gcc/clang, vcpkg, go build, and npm — it just wraps them consistently.

docs.title: Is stoke a replacement for CMake / Meson / Make?
docs.text: Not really. stoke is more like a project runner than a build system. It's opinionated and works out of the box for common cases. For complex build scenarios (cross-compilation, code generation, custom build steps), you probably need CMake.

docs.title: What languages does stoke support?
docs.text:
Currently:

  • Python
  • Java (JDK 17+)
  • C
  • C++
  • Go
  • Rust
  • Kotlin (via Gradle)
  • C# (via the .NET SDK)
  • Ruby
  • PHP
  • JavaScript
  • TypeScript

More languages may come in the future.

docs.title: Which platforms?
docs.text:
• Windows (native installer)
  • Linux (via pip)
  • macOS (via pip)

Actively developed on Windows (MSYS2/MinGW64).

docs.title: How do I update stoke?
docs.text:
Windows installer users: download the new installer and run it. It replaces the old version.

pip users: pip install -U stoke-build.

docs.title: How do I uninstall stoke?
docs.text:
Windows installer: use Windows "Add or Remove Programs" or run the uninstaller in the install directory.

pip: pip uninstall stoke-build.

docs.title: Can I have multiple targets in one project?
docs.text:
Yes. Any number of [targets.<name>] sections:

[targets.server]
language = "python"
entry = "server/main.py"

[targets.client]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["client/**/*.cpp"]

Build all: stoke build Build one: stoke build server

docs.title: Can targets use different languages?
docs.text: Yes. Each target has its own language.

docs.title: Can I share code between targets?
docs.text:
Yes. Adjust sources glob patterns to include shared code:

[targets.server]
language = "python"
sources = ["server/**/*.py", "shared/**/*.py"]

[targets.worker]
language = "python"
sources = ["worker/**/*.py", "shared/**/*.py"]

docs.title: Where's my build output?
docs.text: .stoke/{language}/{target}/{profile}/. See stoke build.

docs.title: Can I add custom build steps?
docs.text: Not directly. stoke doesn't support pre/post-build hooks yet. Wrap stoke build in a shell script if needed.

docs.title: Python: does stoke replace pip / venv?
docs.text: No. stoke uses venv and pip under the hood. It automates the venv creation, dependency installation, and PYTHONPATH setup.

docs.title: Java: does stoke use Maven?
docs.text:
stoke uses Maven Central for dependency downloads. It doesn't use Maven's build system — it invokes javac directly.

The generated pom.xml is for IDE integration only.

docs.title: C/C++: what compiler does stoke use?
docs.text:
• Linux default: gcc
  • macOS default: clang
  • Windows default: gcc (from MSYS2/MinGW)

Override with build profiles. MSVC (cl.exe) is not currently supported.

docs.title: C/C++: can I use CMake?
docs.text: Not through stoke. stoke has its own simple build model. If you need CMake, use CMake directly.

docs.title: Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, PHP: does stoke replace Cargo / Gradle / dotnet / Bundler / Composer?
docs.text: No. stoke delegates directly to each ecosystem's own tool — cargo build/cargo run for Rust, gradlew build/gradlew run for Kotlin, dotnet build/dotnet run for C#, bundle install + ruby/bundle exec ruby for Ruby, composer install + php for PHP. stoke just gives them a consistent stoke build/stoke run interface alongside the other languages.

docs.title: Why don't Rails and Laravel have stoke init scaffolds?
docs.text: Both start via a CLI subcommand (bin/rails server, php artisan serve) rather than by directly executing an entry script, which doesn't fit stoke's current run model (stoke run executes one script/binary). Sinatra (Ruby) and Slim (PHP) were added instead since they fit that model — see the Ruby and PHP language pages for details.

docs.title: Why is my build not using the cache?
docs.text:
Common reasons:

  • Header changed (C/C++ tracks headers automatically)
  • Source file's timestamp changed
  • Compile flags changed (different profile)
  • --force was used

Verbose mode may help debug:

stoke build -v

docs.title: Why does stoke build regenerate IDE files every time?
docs.text:
It doesn't — since v0.7.2. IDE files are only rewritten when their content changes.

If you see IDE files updated: X, Y, only those actually changed.

docs.title: Why is Lock file saved showing every time?
docs.text: Fixed in v0.7.2. Update to the latest version.

docs.title: Does stoke work in CI?
docs.text:
Yes. stoke build in a container or CI runner works the same as locally. Cache the .stoke/ directory to speed up subsequent builds.

Recommended: use lock_mode = "strict" in CI for reproducible builds.

docs.title: Does stoke work with Docker?
docs.text:
Yes. Install stoke in the Dockerfile:

RUN pip install stoke-build

Then stoke build normally.

docs.title: Can I use stoke as a subprocess from another tool?
docs.text:
Yes. Exit codes are meaningful:

  • 0: success
  • non-zero: failure

Output goes to stdout/stderr in the standard way.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and solutions.

docs.title: stoke.toml not found
docs.text:
Cause: You ran stoke from outside a project directory.

Fix: cd into the project root (the directory containing stoke.toml).

docs.title: target 'X' not found in stoke.toml
docs.text:
Cause: The specified target doesn't exist.

Fix: List valid targets by opening stoke.toml. Available targets are shown in the error output.

docs.title: profile 'X' not found
docs.text:
Cause: Custom profile doesn't exist in stoke.toml.

Fix: Check [profiles.*] sections in stoke.toml. Only debug, release, and custom profiles you define are valid.

docs.title: Python X.Y not found
docs.text:
Cause: No Python matching python_version is installed.

Fix:

  1. Check detected Pythons: stoke python list
  2. Install the required Python version, or
  3. Change python_version in stoke.toml to a version you have

docs.title: JDK X not found
docs.text:
Cause: No JDK with the required major version.

Fix:

  1. Check detected JDKs: stoke java list
  2. Install a matching JDK (Adoptium recommended: adoptium.net)
  3. Set JAVA_HOME if needed
  4. Or change java_version in stoke.toml

docs.title: No C compiler detected
docs.text:
Cause: gcc/clang not in PATH.

Fix:

  • Windows: Install MSYS2 and run pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc. Add MSYS2 bin to PATH.
  • macOS: Install Xcode Command Line Tools: xcode-select --install
  • Linux: sudo apt install build-essential (Ubuntu/Debian) or equivalent

docs.title: stoke run fails silently
docs.text:
Cause: The target hasn't been built yet.

Fix: stoke build first.

docs.title: Python: ModuleNotFoundError
docs.text:
Cause: Import paths not set up correctly.

Fix:

  • Ensure each folder has an __init__.py
  • Use full paths from src/: from utils.helpers import ...
  • Check Python source layout

docs.title: Java: Could not find or load main class
docs.text:
Cause: main_class in stoke.toml doesn't match the actual class name.

Fix: Verify the fully qualified class name matches. Example:

// src/main/java/com/example/Main.java
package com.example;
public class Main { ... }

main_class = "com.example.Main"    # fully qualified

docs.title: Stale builds after external changes
docs.text:
Cause: You changed something outside sources (e.g. moved files, changed env vars) and cache is stale.

Fix: Force rebuild:

stoke build --force

docs.title: Lock file mismatch
docs.text:
Cause: Lock file references tools/deps that no longer exist.

Fix: Full reset:

stoke clean --all
stoke build

docs.title: Library install takes forever
docs.text:
Cause: vcpkg builds from source. Some libraries (Boost, Qt) take a very long time.

Fix: Be patient. First install is slow; subsequent uses are fast.

docs.title: Library not found after install
docs.text:
Cause: vcpkg installed the library but stoke's cache is stale.

Fix:

stoke build --force

docs.title: vcpkg corrupted
docs.text:
Cause: Interrupted install or system issue.

Fix:

stoke uninstall vcpkg
stoke install vcpkg
stoke build --force

docs.title: VSCode showing wrong Python interpreter
docs.text:
Cause: VSCode Python extension picked a global Python instead of the venv.

Fix:

  1. stoke build to regenerate .vscode/settings.json
  2. Ctrl+Shift+P → "Python: Select Interpreter" → pick .stoke/python/<target>/venv/

docs.title: VSCode lag on some systems
docs.text:
Cause: File watcher or extensions overloading.

Fix:

  1. Confirm .vscode/settings.json excludes .stoke/
  2. Disable hardware acceleration: settings.json → "disable-hardware-acceleration": true
  3. Disable unused extensions
  4. Restart VSCode

Tracking issue: VSCode lag on some systems

docs.title: C++ IntelliSense not working
docs.text:
Cause: compile_commands.json missing or IDE not picking it up.

Fix:

  1. Run stoke build to generate compile_commands.json
  2. Ensure your extension reads it (Microsoft C/C++ extension reads .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json; clangd reads compile_commands.json)

docs.title: Changes not detected
docs.text:
Cause: Files are outside the sources glob patterns.

Fix: Check sources in stoke.toml covers all your source files.

docs.title: hot-reload doesn't restart
docs.text:
Cause: Process didn't exit cleanly, or output buffered.

Fix:

  • Try again (transient issues)
  • For Python/Java, ensure your program handles SIGTERM/SIGINT properly

docs.title: IDE Integration
docs.text: stoke generates IDE configuration files automatically during stoke build. Open your project in the IDE — everything just works.

docs.title: Supported IDEs
docs.text: IDE Python Java C/C++ VSCode ✓ ✓ ✓ Eclipse ✓ IntelliJ / JetBrains ✓ (via Maven) clangd-based ✓

docs.title: Files generated
docs.text:
Per-project (in project root):

  • .vscode/settings.json

For C/C++: - .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json (Microsoft C/C++ extension) - compile_commands.json (clangd, Native Debug)

For Java: - .classpath (Eclipse format, used by VSCode Java extension) - .project (Eclipse format) - pom.xml (Maven format)

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
settings.json includes:

  • Python: interpreter path, extra paths, exclusions
  • Java: source paths, referenced JARs
  • C/C++: include paths, defines, compiler path

Also excludes .stoke/ from file watching to reduce editor lag.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Recommended VSCode extensions:

  • Python — Microsoft Python extension
  • Java — Extension Pack for Java
  • C/C++ — Microsoft C/C++ extension OR clangd

docs.title: Eclipse (Java)
docs.text:
Import as an existing Eclipse project:

  1. File → Import → General → Existing Projects into Workspace
  2. Select the project folder

Eclipse reads .classpath and .project.

docs.title: IntelliJ / JetBrains (Java)
docs.text:
Import as a Maven project:

  1. File → Open → select the project folder or pom.xml
  2. IntelliJ reads pom.xml

docs.title: clangd (C/C++)
docs.text:
compile_commands.json at the project root is the standard for clangd-based tools:

  • clangd LSP server
  • CLion (via clangd)
  • Neovim + clangd
  • Emacs + clangd
  • Any editor with clangd support

No extra config needed. Just open the project.

docs.title: Multi-project workspaces
docs.text:
For a repository with multiple stoke projects: myworkspace/ ├── frontend/ # python │ └── stoke.toml ├── backend/ # java │ └── stoke.toml └── engine/ # cpp └── stoke.toml

Run in the root:

stoke ide-sync

Generates:

  • .vscode/settings.json — workspace-level settings
  • myworkspace.code-workspace — multi-root VSCode workspace

Open the .code-workspace file to work on all projects together.

See stoke ide-sync for details.

docs.title: Regenerating IDE files
docs.text:
IDE files are regenerated on every stoke build. If they get out of sync (e.g. after changing dependencies), just rebuild:

stoke build

Or force it:

stoke build --force

docs.title: Not modifying manually
docs.text:
Since IDE files are regenerated, manual edits are overwritten on the next build. Configure via stoke.toml instead.

Add extra include paths in stoke.toml:

[targets.myapp]
include_dirs = ["third_party/include"]

docs.title: vcpkg Integration
docs.text: stoke integrates with vcpkg for C/C++ dependency management.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install vcpkg:

stoke install vcpkg

This clones vcpkg into a stoke-managed location and bootstraps it. No admin privileges needed.

Check installation:

stoke vcpkg version

Uninstall:

stoke uninstall vcpkg

docs.title: Installing libraries
docs.text: Two ways:

docs.title: Method 1: Direct install command
docs.text:
stoke vcpkg install fmt
stoke vcpkg install sqlite3

This:

  1. Downloads and builds the library via vcpkg
  2. Adds it to stoke.toml under [targets.<name>.deps]

By default, the library is added to the first target. Specify a target:

stoke vcpkg install fmt --target=engine

docs.title: Method 2: Add to stoke.toml manually
docs.text:
[targets.myapp.deps]
fmt = "*"
sqlite3 = "*"

Then run:

stoke build

stoke automatically installs any declared but missing libraries.

docs.title: Removing libraries
docs.text:
stoke vcpkg remove fmt

This:

  1. Removes from stoke.toml
  2. Runs vcpkg's remove command

docs.title: Listing installed libraries
docs.text:
stoke vcpkg list

Or for a specific target:

stoke vcpkg list --target=engine

docs.title: Specific versions
docs.text:
Install a specific version:

stoke vcpkg install fmt --version=10.1.1

Or in stoke.toml:

[targets.myapp.deps]
fmt = "10.1.1"

Use "*" for the latest available:

[targets.myapp.deps]
fmt = "*"

docs.title: How stoke uses vcpkg
docs.text:
At build time:

  1. stoke reads [targets.<name>.deps]
  2. Verifies each library is installed via vcpkg
  3. Adds vcpkg include paths (e.g. installed/x64-mingw-dynamic/include/) to compile flags
  4. Links vcpkg library files (.a, .lib, .so, etc.) at link time

Include paths and library paths are automatic. In your code:

#include <fmt/format.h>          // works, no extra config needed

docs.title: Language compatibility
docs.text:
Some libraries are C-only, some are C++-only.

C project:

[targets.myapp]
language = "c"

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"    # ✓ C library
fmt = "*"        # ✗ C++ only, stoke will error

C++ project:

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"    # ✓ works (C libraries usable from C++)
fmt = "*"        # ✓ C++ library

stoke validates compatibility before installing.

docs.title: Triplets
docs.text:
vcpkg builds libraries per triplet (architecture + platform + linkage).

Auto-detected default:

  • Windows MinGW64: x64-mingw-dynamic
  • Windows MSVC: x64-windows
  • Linux x64: x64-linux
  • macOS: x64-osx or arm64-osx

Stored in .stoke/lock.toml per dependency.

docs.title: Library not found after install
docs.text: Try stoke build --force to clear the cache and re-scan vcpkg.

docs.title: Long install times
docs.text: First install of some libraries (like Boost, Qt) can take an hour. This is vcpkg building from source. Subsequent builds are fast.

docs.title: Reset vcpkg
docs.text:
If vcpkg gets corrupted:

stoke uninstall vcpkg
stoke install vcpkg
stoke build --force

docs.title: stoke build
docs.text: Build a target.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
stoke build [target] [options]

If target is omitted, the first target in stoke.toml is used.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --force Ignore cache and rebuild everything --debug Build with the debug profile (default) --release Build with the release profile --profile <name> Build with a custom profile from stoke.toml -v, --verbose Show detailed build output

docs.title: Basic build
docs.text:
stoke build

Builds the default target with the debug profile.

docs.title: Specify target
docs.text:
stoke build myapp

Builds the myapp target.

docs.title: Release build
docs.text:
stoke build --release

Optimized build (-O2 for C/C++, defines NDEBUG).

docs.title: Custom profile
docs.text:
# stoke.toml
[profiles.small]
compile_flags = ["-Os", "-flto"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

stoke build --profile=small

docs.title: Force rebuild
docs.text:
stoke build --force

Ignores the cache and recompiles everything. Useful when you suspect stale artifacts.

docs.title: Verbose output
docs.text:
stoke build -v

Shows compiler paths, per-file compilation status, and detailed steps.

docs.title: Output structure
docs.text:
Build artifacts are organized by language, target, and profile: .stoke/ ├── {language}/ │ └── {target}/ │ └── {profile}/ │ ├── objects/ # C/C++ .o files │ ├── classes/ # Java .class files │ └── {target}.exe # Final executable ├── cache.json # Incremental build cache └── lock.toml # Locked versions

Example for a C project: .stoke/ ├── c/ │ └── myapp/ │ ├── debug/ │ │ ├── objects/ │ │ └── myapp.exe │ └── release/ │ ├── objects/ │ └── myapp.exe ├── cache.json └── lock.toml

docs.title: Incremental compilation
docs.text:
stoke tracks file modifications and header dependencies. Only changed files are recompiled.

For C/C++, header dependencies are tracked via gcc's -MMD flag. If header.h changes, all files that #include "header.h" (directly or indirectly) will be recompiled.

To bypass the cache, use --force.

docs.title: Build profiles
docs.text:
Default profiles:

  • debug — -O0 -g -Wall, defines DEBUG (C/C++ only)
  • release — -O2, defines NDEBUG (C/C++ only)

Note: profiles only affect C/C++ builds. Python and Java ignore profiles.

Custom profiles are defined in stoke.toml:

[profiles.myprofile]
compile_flags = ["-O3", "-march=native"]
defines = { MYFLAG = 1 }
compiler = "clang"  # optional: override compiler

See Profiles for details.

docs.title: stoke clean
docs.text: Delete build artifacts.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
stoke clean [target] [options]

If target is omitted, all targets are cleaned.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --all Also delete the lock file (full reset)

docs.title: Clean all targets
docs.text:
stoke clean

Removes:

  • .stoke/{language}/{target}/ for each target (Kotlin is the exception — it uses Gradle's own build/ directory at the project root instead, which stoke clean also removes)
  • .stoke/cache.json
  • All __pycache__ folders in the project

docs.title: Clean a specific target
docs.text:
stoke clean myapp

Only removes artifacts for myapp.

docs.title: Full reset
docs.text:
stoke clean --all

Also deletes .stoke/lock.toml, forcing dependency re-resolution on the next build.

Use this if: - Lock file is corrupted - You want to pull the latest versions of dependencies - Switching Python/JDK versions caused issues

docs.title: What gets deleted
docs.text:
Item clean clean --all Object files (.o, .class) ✓ ✓ Executables ✓ ✓ Python venv ✓ ✓ .stoke/cache.json ✓ ✓ __pycache__/ ✓ ✓ .stoke/lock.toml ✓ IDE files (.vscode/, .classpath, etc.)

IDE files are never deleted; they're regenerated on the next build.

docs.title: After clean
docs.text:
Next build will:

  • Recompile everything (no cache)
  • Recreate the Python venv (if applicable)
  • Reinstall dependencies (with --all)

docs.text: • stoke build --force — force rebuild without deleting artifacts

docs.title: stoke hot-reload
docs.text: Watch for file changes, rebuild, and restart the running process.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: stoke hot-reload [target] [options]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --debug Debug build (default) --release Release build --profile <name> Custom profile -v, --verbose Show detailed build output

docs.title: Example
docs.text: stoke hot-reload

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
[hot-reload] Rebuilding 'myapp'... Using c compiler 15.2.0 Compiled 1 file(s) Build complete: myapp [hot-reload] Starting: .stoke\cpp\myapp\debug\myapp.exe [hot-reload] Watching: C:\myproject\src [hot-reload] Press Ctrl+C to stop. Hello from stoke!

When you save a file, stoke stops the process, rebuilds, and restarts: [hot-reload] Detected changes in: src\main.c [hot-reload] Stopping process... ================================================== [hot-reload] Rebuilding 'myapp'... Using c compiler 15.2.0 Compiled 1 file(s) Build complete: myapp [hot-reload] Starting: .stoke\cpp\myapp\debug\myapp.exe Hello from stoke!

Press Ctrl+C to stop the watcher and the process.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Best for long-running processes:

  • Web servers (Flask, Spring Boot, etc.)
  • Development scripts with state
  • Background workers

For batch programs that finish and exit quickly, stoke watch is usually enough.

docs.title: Language-specific behavior
docs.text:
Same as stoke run:

  • Python: runs the entry script
  • Java: runs main_class
  • C/C++: runs the compiled executable

docs.title: C/C++ note
docs.text:
For C/C++, stoke stops the process before rebuilding. This is necessary because the linker can't overwrite a running executable on most platforms.

For Python and Java, stoke rebuilds first and stops the process after, since there's no such limitation.

docs.title: stoke ide-sync
docs.text: Generate IDE configurations for a multi-project workspace.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Run from a directory that contains multiple stoke projects:

stoke ide-sync

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Scans subdirectories for stoke.toml files and generates:

  • .vscode/settings.json — VSCode workspace settings
  • {workspace_name}.code-workspace — VSCode multi-root workspace file

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Directory structure: myworkspace/ ├── frontend/ │ └── stoke.toml # python ├── backend/ │ └── stoke.toml # java └── engine/ └── stoke.toml # cpp

Run: $ cd myworkspace $ stoke ide-sync Scanning for stoke projects under C:\Users...\myworkspace... Found 3 project(s): [python] frontend [java] backend [cpp] engine Generated: C:\Users...\myworkspace.vscode\settings.json Generated: C:\Users...\myworkspace\myworkspace.code-workspace Open in VSCode: C:\Users...\myworkspace\myworkspace.code-workspace

Open the .code-workspace file in VSCode to work on all projects together with proper language support for each.

docs.title: stoke init
docs.text: Create a new stoke project interactively.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
stoke init

Runs an interactive wizard in the current directory.

stoke init <framework>

Skips the wizard and scaffolds a specific framework directly (e.g. stoke init fastapi, stoke init gin). See Framework scaffolding for the full list.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The wizard asks:

  1. Project name — defaults to the current folder name
  2. Language — Python, Java, C, C++, Go, Rust, Kotlin, C#, Ruby, PHP, JavaScript, or TypeScript
  3. Language version — Python 3.12, Java 25, C11, C++20, etc. (Go/JavaScript/TypeScript have no version prompt at all — they use whatever toolchain is on PATH; Kotlin prompts for a JDK version, reusing the Java detection; Rust/C#/Ruby/PHP prompt for an optional toolchain version pin — see Non-interactive mode and the language pages for what gets generated)
  4. Entry point / main class — depending on the language
  5. Dependencies — optional

Then it generates:

  • stoke.toml — project configuration
  • src/ — source directory
  • A hello-world source file

docs.title: Example: C++ project
docs.text:
$ mkdir myapp && cd myapp $ stoke init Project name [myapp]: Language [python/java/c/cpp]: cpp C++ standard [17/20/23] [20]: Executable name [myapp]: Install vcpkg for C/C++ library management? [y/N]: n Created: stoke.toml src/main.cpp Try: stoke build stoke run

Generated stoke.toml:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["src/**/*.cpp"]
cpp_standard = "c++20"

docs.title: Example: Python project
docs.text:
$ mkdir myapp && cd myapp $ stoke init Project name [myapp]: Language [python/java/c/cpp]: python Python version [3.10/3.11/3.12/3.13]: 3.12 Entry file [src/main.py]: Created: stoke.toml src/main.py

Generated stoke.toml:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "python"
python_version = "3.12"
entry = "src/main.py"
sources = ["src/**/*.py"]

docs.title: Example: Java project
docs.text:
$ mkdir myapp && cd myapp $ stoke init Project name [myapp]: Language [python/java/c/cpp]: java Java version [17/21/25]: 25 Package [com.myapp]: Main class [Main]: Created: stoke.toml src/main/java/com/myapp/Main.java

Generated stoke.toml:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "java"
java_version = "25"
sources = ["src/main/java/**/*.java"]
main_class = "com.myapp.Main"

docs.title: Non-interactive mode (CI / team onboarding)
docs.text:
For scripts, CI, or scaffolding tools where prompts aren't an option, pass --language and stoke skips the wizard entirely:

stoke init --language=rust --name=myapp --version=1.75.0 --lock-mode=commit --yes
Flag Meaning --language Required. One of: python, java, c, cpp, go, rust, kotlin, csharp, ruby, php, javascript, typescript --name Project name. Defaults to the current folder name --version Meaning depends on the language (see table below). Omit to use a sensible default --env-type venv or conda. Python only, defaults to venv --lock-mode commit or local. Defaults to commit --vcpkg Install vcpkg if not already present. C/C++ only --yes Overwrite an existing stoke.toml without prompting. Without this flag, init fails loudly if stoke.toml already exists — safer for scripts than silently clobbering a teammate's config

--version per language:

Language --version means Default if omitted Python Python version (e.g. 3.12) System's default detected install Java JDK version (e.g. 21) System's default detected install Kotlin JDK version, written as java_version in stoke.toml System's default detected install C C standard (e.g. c17) c17 C++ C++ standard (e.g. c++20) c++17 Rust Optional toolchain pin, written to rust-toolchain.toml Not written (no pin) C# Optional SDK pin, written to global.json Not written (no pin) Ruby Optional version pin, written to .ruby-version Not written (no pin) PHP Optional version constraint, written into composer.json's require.php Not written (no pin) Go, JavaScript, TypeScript Not used —

Exit codes are meaningful (0 success, non-zero failure), so this composes cleanly in onboarding scripts:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
mkdir myapp && cd myapp
stoke init --language=python --version=3.12 --lock-mode=commit --yes
stoke build

docs.title: Version pinning for team consistency
docs.text:
Rust, C#, Ruby, and PHP don't have their own version-manager concept the way Python/Java do in stoke, so stoke init can optionally write the ecosystem's own standard pin file — committed to git, it makes every teammate's stoke build use (or fail loudly without) the same toolchain version:

  • Rust → rust-toolchain.toml (read automatically by rustup)
  • C# → global.json (read automatically by the dotnet CLI)
  • Ruby → .ruby-version (read automatically by rbenv/rvm/asdf/chruby)
  • PHP → composer.json's require.php constraint (enforced by composer install, which runs as part of stoke build once composer.json exists)
  • Kotlin → the existing java_version field in stoke.toml is enforced by stoke itself: stoke build/stoke run resolve a matching JDK and pass it to Gradle via -Dorg.gradle.java.home, failing with a clear error if no matching JDK is installed

These prompts are optional in the interactive wizard (leave blank to skip) and only apply when --version is passed in non-interactive mode.

stoke build --verbose

docs.title: stoke run
docs.text: Run the built target.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
stoke run [target] [options]

If target is omitted, the first target in stoke.toml is used.

stoke run does not rebuild. It runs the previously built artifact. Run stoke build first if you've made changes.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --debug Run the debug build (default) --release Run the release build --profile <name> Run a specific custom profile build

docs.title: Basic run
docs.text:
stoke run

Runs the default target with the debug profile.

docs.title: Specify target
docs.text: stoke run myapp

docs.title: Run release build
docs.text:
stoke build --release
stoke run --release

docs.title: Run custom profile
docs.text:
stoke build --profile=small
stoke run --profile=small

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Runs the entry script with the project's venv:

[targets.myapp]
language = "python"
entry = "src/main.py"
$ stoke run Running: C:\myproject\src\main.py Hello from stoke!

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
Runs the class specified by main_class:

[targets.myapp]
language = "java"
main_class = "com.example.Main"
$ stoke run Running: com.example.Main Hello from stoke!

The classpath includes compiled .class files and Maven dependencies.

docs.title: C / C++
docs.text: Runs the compiled executable: $ stoke run Running: .stoke\cpp\myapp\debug\myapp.exe Hello from stoke!

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: The exit code of stoke run matches the target's exit code. If your program returns non-zero, stoke run also returns non-zero.

docs.title: stoke watch
docs.text: Watch for file changes and rebuild automatically.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: stoke watch [target] [options]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description --debug Debug build (default) --release Release build --profile <name> Custom profile -v, --verbose Show detailed build output

docs.title: Example
docs.text: stoke watch

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
[watch] Rebuilding 'myapp'... Using c compiler 15.2.0 Compiled 1 file(s) Build complete: myapp [watch] Watching: C:\myproject\src [watch] Press Ctrl+C to stop.

When you save a file, stoke automatically rebuilds: [watch] Detected changes in: src\main.c ================================================== [watch] Rebuilding 'myapp'... Using c compiler 15.2.0 Compiled 1 file(s) Build complete: myapp

Press Ctrl+C to stop.

docs.title: What's watched
docs.text:
stoke watches the directories that contain your sources patterns. For example, with:

[targets.myapp]
sources = ["src/**/*.c"]

stoke watches src/.

Only files matching the source extensions for your language are considered:

  • Python: .py
  • Java: .java
  • C: .c, .h
  • C++: .cpp, .hpp, .h

Other file changes are ignored.

docs.title: Debouncing
docs.text: Multiple rapid changes are debounced. If you save 5 files in quick succession, stoke rebuilds once, not 5 times.

docs.title: Profiles work with watch
docs.text:
Watch respects the profile you choose:

stoke watch --release

Builds into .stoke/{lang}/{target}/release/ on every change.

docs.text:

  • stoke build — single build

docs.title: Lock File
docs.text: .stoke/lock.toml records the exact versions of tools and dependencies used in each build. It ensures reproducibility: another developer (or CI) building your project gets the same versions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Reproducibility: same versions across machines
  • Speed: skip re-resolving dependencies if lock matches
  • Auditability: see exactly what versions your build uses

docs.title: Location
docs.text: myproject/ ├── stoke.toml └── .stoke/ └── lock.toml # ← lock file

docs.title: Should you commit it?
docs.text:
Yes for applications, no for libraries.

  • Application: commit lock.toml to git. This pins versions so all developers and CI use the same versions.
  • Library: don't commit. Let users of the library resolve fresh versions.

Add to .gitignore for libraries: .stoke/lock.toml

docs.title: Build Profiles
docs.text: Build profiles let you switch between different build configurations without editing your code. Currently supported for C and C++ only.

docs.title: Built-in profiles
docs.text: stoke provides two default profiles:

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
compile_flags = ["-O0", "-g", "-Wall"]
defines = { DEBUG = 1 }

Default when you run stoke build. Good for development:

  • No optimization (-O0)
  • Full debug info (-g)
  • All warnings enabled (-Wall)
  • DEBUG defined for conditional compilation

docs.title: release
docs.text:
compile_flags = ["-O2"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

Use with --release:

  • Optimization (-O2)
  • NDEBUG defined (disables assert(), etc.)

docs.title: Using profiles
docs.text:
stoke build                     # debug (default)
stoke build --debug             # debug (explicit)
stoke build --release           # release
stoke build --profile=    # custom profile

Corresponding stoke run and stoke watch:

stoke run --release
stoke watch --profile=custom
stoke hot-reload --release

docs.title: Custom profiles
docs.text:
Define custom profiles in stoke.toml:

[profiles.<name>]
compile_flags = [...]     # extra compiler flags
defines = { KEY = value } # preprocessor defines
compiler = "..."          # optional: override compiler

docs.title: Example: size-optimized
docs.text:
[profiles.small]
compile_flags = ["-Os", "-flto", "-s"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

stoke build --profile=small

docs.title: Example: native optimization
docs.text:
[profiles.native]
compile_flags = ["-O3", "-march=native"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1, NATIVE_BUILD = 1 }

docs.title: Example: clang override
docs.text:
[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"
compile_flags = ["-O2", "-Wall", "-Wextra"]

The compiler field overrides the default compiler for this profile. Value: "gcc" or "clang".

docs.title: Output directories
docs.text:
Each profile builds into its own directory: .stoke/ └── cpp/ └── myapp/ ├── debug/ │ └── myapp.exe ├── release/ │ └── myapp.exe └── small/ └── myapp.exe

Rebuilding a different profile doesn't affect others. You can maintain multiple builds simultaneously.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
You can't combine flag styles:

stoke build --debug --release           # error: can't combine
stoke build --release --profile=small   # error: can't combine

docs.title: Not available for Python/Java
docs.text: Profiles apply to C/C++ only. Python and Java builds ignore the profile flag but still use profile-based output directories: .stoke/ ├── python/ │ └── myapp/ │ └── venv/ # same venv regardless of profile └── java/ └── myapp/ └── debug/ # default profile dir └── classes/

docs.title: Available flags
docs.text:
Profile fields:

Field Type Description compile_flags list[string] Extra flags for the compiler defines table Preprocessor -D defines compiler string Override compiler ("gcc" or "clang")

docs.title: stoke.toml Reference
docs.text: Complete reference for the stoke.toml configuration file.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["src/**/*.cpp"]

[targets.myapp.deps]
fmt = "*"

[profiles.custom]
compile_flags = ["-O2"]

Sections:

  • [project] — project-wide metadata
  • [targets.<name>] — one section per build target
  • [targets.<name>.deps] — dependencies for a target
  • [profiles.<name>] — build profiles (C/C++ only)

docs.title: [project]
docs.text:
Project-level configuration.

[project]
name = "myapp"           # Required. Project name.
version = "0.1.0"        # Optional. Project version.
lock_mode = "auto"       # Optional. Lock file behavior.
jobs = 4                 # Optional. Default parallel build workers.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description name string Project name version string Semver-ish version lock_mode "auto" | "strict" | "off" Lock file behavior (default: "auto") jobs int Default parallel workers for build (C/C++)

docs.title: lock_mode values
docs.text:
• "auto": use lock file if present, update as needed
  • "strict": require lock file, fail if versions don't match
  • "off": don't use or write lock file

docs.title: [targets.<name>]
docs.text:
One section per build target. Multiple targets allowed:

[targets.server]
language = "python"
entry = "src/server.py"

[targets.worker]
language = "python"
entry = "src/worker.py"

Build a specific target:

stoke build server
stoke run worker

If no target is specified, the first one in the file is used.

docs.title: Common fields
docs.text: Field Required Description language Yes "python", "java", "c", "cpp" sources Depends Glob patterns for source files

docs.title: Python-specific fields
docs.text: Field Description python_version Required Python version entry Entry script path

docs.title: Java-specific fields
docs.text: Field Description java_version Required JDK major version main_class Fully qualified main class

docs.title: C/C++-specific fields
docs.text: Field Description c_standard C standard ("c11", "c17", etc.) cpp_standard C++ standard ("c++17", "c++20", etc.) include_dirs Extra include directories jobs Override project-level jobs

docs.title: [targets.<name>.deps]
docs.text: Dependencies for a specific target. Format varies by language.

docs.title: Python (pip)
docs.text:
[targets.myapp.deps]
requests = "*"
flask = ">=2.0"
numpy = "==1.24.3"
mypackage = "git+https://github.com/user/repo"

docs.title: Java (Maven)
docs.text:
[targets.myapp.deps]
"com.google.code.gson:gson" = "2.10.1"
"org.slf4j:slf4j-api" = "2.0.9"

Key format: "groupId:artifactId".

docs.title: C / C++ (vcpkg)
docs.text:
[targets.myapp.deps]
fmt = "*"
sqlite3 = "*"

Version is passed to vcpkg. "*" means latest available.

docs.title: [profiles.<name>]
docs.text:
Build profiles for C/C++.

[profiles.small]
compile_flags = ["-Os", "-flto"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"

See Profiles for the full reference.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
Multi-target project:

[project]
name = "myservice"
version = "1.0.0"

# Python backend
[targets.backend]
language = "python"
python_version = "3.12"
entry = "backend/main.py"
sources = ["backend/**/*.py"]

[targets.backend.deps]
fastapi = "*"
uvicorn = "*"

# C++ engine
[targets.engine]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["engine/src/**/*.cpp"]
cpp_standard = "c++20"
include_dirs = ["engine/include"]
jobs = 8

[targets.engine.deps]
fmt = "*"
spdlog = "*"

# Custom profile
[profiles.native]
compile_flags = ["-O3", "-march=native"]

Build individual targets:

stoke build backend
stoke build engine --profile=native

  • 템플릿 추가: src/app/templates/에 .html 파일 생성
  • 정적 파일 추가: src/app/static/에 CSS/JS/이미지 배치

docs.title: Gin
docs.text:
Gin 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init gin

Gin은 Go의 인기 있는 고성능 HTTP 웹 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text:
• Project name: 프로젝트 디렉토리 이름
  • Go module name: 예: github.com/user/myapp (기본값은 프로젝트 이름)

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
myapp/
├── stoke.toml
├── go.mod
├── main.go                    # Gin 진입점
└── handlers/
    └── hello.go               # 샘플 핸들러

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: • github.com/gin-gonic/gin (go get으로 설치)

docs.title: 기본 설정
docs.text:
• Port: 8080
  • Endpoints:
  • GET / → {"message": "Hello from Gin + stoke!"}
  • GET /hello/:name → {"message": "Hello, {name}!"}

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
cd myapp
stoke build
stoke run

브라우저: http://localhost:8080/

docs.title: 커스터마이징
docs.text:
• 포트 변경: main.go의 r.Run(":8080") 수정
  • 핸들러 추가: handlers/에 파일 생성, main.go에서 등록
  • 미들웨어 추가: main.go의 r.Use(...) 사용

docs.title: Hono
docs.text:
Hono 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init hono

Hono는 엣지 컴퓨팅(Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun, Node.js)을 위한 가볍고 빠른 웹 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text:
stoke는 npm create hono@latest를 호출하며 다음을 물어봅니다:

  • Project name
  • Template: Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Pages, Deno, Bun, Node.js, Vercel, AWS Lambda 등
  • Package manager

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text: 템플릿(엣지 플랫폼)에 따라 다름.

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: Hono 코어 + 플랫폼별 의존성.

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
stoke가 관리하지 않음 — 플랫폼별 명령어 사용:

cd myapp
npm install
npm run dev

포트와 URL은 선택한 플랫폼에 따라 다름 (Cloudflare Workers는 보통 http://localhost:8787/).

docs.title: 참고
docs.text:
• stoke는 Hono 프로젝트를 빌드하거나 실행하지 않음
  • Hono는 엣지 런타임에 최적화됨
  • Node.js, Deno, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, AWS Lambda 호환
  • 자세한 내용은 Hono 공식 문서 참조

docs.title: Ktor
docs.text:
Ktor 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init ktor

Ktor는 JetBrains가 만든 경량, 코루틴 기반 Kotlin 웹 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text: • Project name: 프로젝트 디렉토리 이름

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
myapp/
├── stoke.toml
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── build.gradle.kts
├── gradlew / gradlew.bat      # gradle이 있으면 wrapper 생성
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── kotlin/
            └── Main.kt        # Ktor 진입점

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text:
• io.ktor:ktor-server-core-jvm 2.3.12
  • io.ktor:ktor-server-netty-jvm 2.3.12 (Netty 엔진)

docs.title: 기본 설정
docs.text:
• Port: 8080
  • Endpoints:
  • GET / → Hello from Ktor + stoke!
  • GET /hello/{name} → Hello, {name}!

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
cd myapp
stoke build
stoke run

브라우저: http://localhost:8080/

docs.title: 커스터마이징
docs.text:
• 포트 변경: src/main/kotlin/Main.kt의 embeddedServer(Netty, port = 8080) 수정
  • 라우트 추가: routing { ... } 블록 안에 추가
  • 플러그인 추가: embeddedServer { ... } 안에서 Ktor 플러그인(ContentNegotiation, CORS 등) 설치

docs.title: NestJS
docs.text:
NestJS 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init nestjs

NestJS는 Angular 스타일 아키텍처 (모듈, 컨트롤러, 서비스)를 사용하는 TypeScript 백엔드 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text:
• Project name
  • Package manager: npm / yarn / pnpm (NestJS CLI)

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
표준 NestJS 구조:

myapp/
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts
│   ├── app.module.ts
│   ├── app.controller.ts
│   └── app.service.ts
├── test/
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── nest-cli.json

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: 표준 NestJS 의존성 (@nestjs/common, @nestjs/core, rxjs 등).

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
stoke가 관리하지 않음 — NestJS 명령어 직접 사용:

cd myapp
npm run start:dev     # 개발 (핫 리로드)
npm run build         # 프로덕션 빌드
npm run start:prod    # 프로덕션 서버

브라우저: http://localhost:3000/

docs.title: 참고
docs.text:
• stoke는 NestJS 프로젝트를 빌드하거나 실행하지 않음
  • 모듈 추가: nest g module <name>
  • 컨트롤러 추가: nest g controller <name>
  • 자세한 내용은 NestJS 공식 문서 참조

docs.title: Next.js
docs.text:
Next.js 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init nextjs

Next.js는 SSR, SSG, 파일 기반 라우팅을 지원하는 React 풀스택 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text:
stoke는 create-next-app을 호출하며 다음을 물어봅니다:

  • Project name
  • TypeScript?
  • ESLint?
  • Tailwind CSS?
  • src/ directory?
  • App Router?
  • Turbopack?
  • Import alias?

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text: 표준 Next.js 구조 (옵션에 따라 다름). package.json, next.config.ts, app/ 또는 pages/ 등.

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: 표준 Next.js 의존성 (Next.js, React, TypeScript 선택 시).

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
stoke가 관리하지 않음 — Next.js 명령어 직접 사용:

cd myapp
npm run dev         # 개발 서버
npm run build       # 프로덕션 빌드
npm start           # 프로덕션 서버

브라우저: http://localhost:3000/

docs.title: 참고
docs.text:
• stoke는 Next.js 프로젝트를 빌드하거나 실행하지 않음
  • Next.js는 React 애플리케이션에 최적화된 자체 빌드 시스템 사용
  • 자세한 내용은 Next.js 공식 문서 참조

docs.title: Nuxt
docs.text:
Nuxt 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init nuxt

Nuxt는 SSR, SSG, 파일 기반 라우팅을 지원하는 Vue.js 풀스택 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text:
stoke는 nuxi init을 호출하며 다음을 물어봅니다:

  • Template: minimal 등
  • Package manager: npm / yarn / pnpm / bun
  • Initialize git repository?

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
표준 Nuxt 구조:

myapp/
├── app.vue
├── nuxt.config.ts
├── package.json
└── (pages/, components/, etc.)

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: 표준 Nuxt 의존성 (nuxt, vue).

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
stoke가 관리하지 않음 — Nuxt 명령어 직접 사용:

cd myapp
npm install
npm run dev         # 개발 서버
npm run build       # 프로덕션 빌드
npm run preview     # 프로덕션 미리보기

브라우저: http://localhost:3000/

docs.title: 참고
docs.text:
• stoke는 Nuxt 프로젝트를 빌드하거나 실행하지 않음
  • Nuxt는 Next.js와 비슷한 파일 기반 라우팅을 Vue에서 사용
  • 자세한 내용은 Nuxt 공식 문서 참조

docs.title: 프레임워크 스캐폴딩
docs.text:
stoke는 인기 프레임워크의 실행 가능한 프로젝트를 명령어 하나로 생성합니다:

# Java
stoke init spring-boot

# Python
stoke init fastapi
stoke init flask
stoke init django

# Go
stoke init gin
stoke init echo
stoke init fiber
stoke init chi

# JavaScript
stoke init express
stoke init fastify

# TypeScript
stoke init nextjs
stoke init nestjs
stoke init vite
stoke init nuxt
stoke init sveltekit
stoke init hono

# Rust
stoke init actix-web
stoke init axum
stoke init rocket

# Kotlin
stoke init ktor
stoke init spring-boot-kotlin

# C#
stoke init aspnet-core

# Ruby
stoke init sinatra

# PHP
stoke init slim

각 명령어는 기본 설정을 대화형으로 받고 샘플 코드와 함께 프로젝트 구조를 생성합니다.

docs.title: Java
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init spring-boot Spring Boot (Spring Initializr 사용)

docs.title: Python
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init fastapi FastAPI + uvicorn stoke init flask Flask + Jinja2 템플릿 stoke init django Django (프로젝트 + 앱 전체 구조)

docs.title: Go
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init gin Gin — 인기 있는 고성능 HTTP 프레임워크 stoke init echo Echo — 미니멀, 고성능 stoke init fiber Fiber — Express 스타일 API stoke init chi Chi — 표준 라이브러리 기반 경량 라우터

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init express Express — 클래식 Node.js 웹 프레임워크 stoke init fastify Fastify — 빠르고 오버헤드 적음

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init nextjs Next.js — React 풀스택 stoke init nestjs NestJS — Angular 스타일 백엔드 stoke init vite Vite — 빠른 프론트엔드 빌드 도구 stoke init nuxt Nuxt — Vue 풀스택 stoke init sveltekit SvelteKit — Svelte 풀스택 stoke init hono Hono — 엣지 컴퓨팅 프레임워크

docs.title: Rust
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init actix-web Actix-web — 성숙하고 고성능인 프레임워크 stoke init axum Axum — Tokio 팀이 만든 Tokio 기반 프레임워크 stoke init rocket Rocket — 사용 편의성 중심 프레임워크

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init ktor Ktor — 경량, 코루틴 기반 프레임워크 stoke init spring-boot-kotlin Kotlin DSL + kotlin-spring 플러그인 사용 Spring Boot

docs.title: C
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init aspnet-core ASP.NET Core — minimal API 템플릿

docs.title: Ruby
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init sinatra Sinatra — 경량 웹 앱 DSL

docs.title: PHP
docs.text: 명령어 프레임워크 stoke init slim Slim Framework — 경량 PSR-7 마이크로 프레임워크

docs.title: 생성되는 것
docs.text:
각 프레임워크별 페이지에서 확인:

Java: - Spring Boot

Python: - FastAPI - Flask - Django

Go: - Gin - Echo - Fiber - Chi

JavaScript: - Express - Fastify

TypeScript: - Next.js - NestJS - Vite - Nuxt - SvelteKit - Hono

Rust: - Actix-web - Axum - Rocket

Kotlin: - Ktor - Spring Boot (Kotlin)

C#: - ASP.NET Core

Ruby: - Sinatra

PHP: - Slim Framework

docs.title: 스캐폴딩 후
docs.text:
Python, Go, JavaScript 프레임워크 (Express, Fastify), Rust, Ruby (Sinatra)는 동일한 워크플로우:

stoke build
stoke run

Spring Boot (Java 또는 Kotlin)는 Maven 또는 Gradle 사용:

mvnw spring-boot:run       # Linux/macOS (Java, Maven)
mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run   # Windows (Java, Maven)
gradlew bootRun            # Linux/macOS (Kotlin, 또는 Java+Gradle)
gradlew.bat bootRun        # Windows

Kotlin (Ktor)과 C# (ASP.NET Core)는 위 컴파일 언어들과 동일하게 stoke build / stoke run 그대로 사용.

PHP (Slim)은 stoke build 이후 PHP 내장 개발 서버가 필요 — Slim 프레임워크 페이지 참조.

TypeScript 프레임워크 (Next.js, NestJS, Vite, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Hono)는 각 프레임워크 명령어 사용:

npm run dev     # 개발
npm run build   # 프로덕션

stoke는 공식 스캐폴딩 도구 (create-next-app, @nestjs/cli, nuxi, sv create 등)를 호출하므로 최신 프로젝트 템플릿을 얻습니다.

docs.title: Rocket
docs.text:
Rocket 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init rocket

Rocket은 사용 편의성에 중점을 둔 Rust 웹 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text: • Project name: 프로젝트 디렉토리 이름

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
myapp/
├── stoke.toml
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    └── main.rs           # Rocket 진입점

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: • rocket 0.5

docs.title: 기본 설정
docs.text:
• Port: 8000 (Rocket 기본값)
  • Endpoints:
  • GET / → Hello from Rocket + stoke!
  • GET /hello/<name> → Hello, {name}!

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
cd myapp
stoke build
stoke run

브라우저: http://localhost:8000/

docs.title: 커스터마이징
docs.text:
• 포트 변경: Rocket.toml에 [default] port = <port> 추가하거나 ROCKET_PORT 환경변수 설정
  • 라우트 추가: #[get(...)] 어노테이션 함수 추가 후 routes![...]에 등록
  • state/fairing 추가: rocket::build()에 .manage(...) / .attach(...) 사용

docs.title: Sinatra
docs.text:
Sinatra 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init sinatra

Sinatra는 Ruby로 웹 앱을 만드는 경량 DSL입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text: • Project name: 프로젝트 디렉토리 이름

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
myapp/
├── stoke.toml
├── Gemfile
└── src/
    └── main.rb           # Sinatra 진입점

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text: • sinatra ~> 4.0 (Gemfile에 선언, bundle install로 설치)

docs.title: 기본 설정
docs.text:
• Port: 4567 (Sinatra 기본값, set :port, 4567로 명시)
  • Endpoints:
  • GET / → Hello from Sinatra + stoke!
  • GET /hello/:name → Hello, {name}!

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
cd myapp
stoke build
stoke run

브라우저: http://localhost:4567/

docs.title: 커스터마이징
docs.text:
• 포트 변경: src/main.rb의 set :port, 4567 수정
  • 라우트 추가: get "/path" do ... end / post "/path" do ... end 블록 추가
  • gem 추가: Gemfile에 추가 후 stoke build로 bundle install

docs.title: 왜 Rails가 아닌가
docs.text: Rails 앱은 별도 CLI 서브커맨드인 bin/rails server로 실행됩니다 — entry 스크립트를 직접 실행하는 방식이 아니에요. 이건 지금 stoke의 실행 모델(ruby <entry> / bundle exec ruby <entry>)에 안 맞아서, stoke run을 돌리면 서버가 안 뜨고 Rails CLI 도움말만 찍힙니다. Sinatra는 classic 스타일 앱이 entry 파일 실행 즉시 자체 서버를 띄우는 구조라 이 모델에 정확히 맞습니다.

docs.title: Slim Framework
docs.text:
Slim Framework 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init slim

Slim은 PHP용 경량 PSR-7 마이크로 프레임워크입니다.

docs.title: 프롬프트
docs.text: • Project name: 프로젝트 디렉토리 이름

docs.title: 생성 파일
docs.text:
myapp/
├── stoke.toml
├── composer.json
└── public/
    └── index.php          # Slim 진입점

docs.title: 의존성
docs.text:
• slim/slim ^4.0
  • slim/psr7 ^1.6 (PSR-7 구현체)

docs.title: 기본 설정
docs.text:
• Endpoints:
  • GET / → Hello from Slim + stoke!
  • GET /hello/{name} → Hello, {name}!

docs.title: 실행
docs.text:
Slim은 Sinatra처럼 스스로 서버를 띄우는 구조가 아니라서, PHP 내장 개발 서버가 필요합니다 — stoke run만으로는 부족합니다:

cd myapp
composer install               # 스캐폴딩 중 이미 실행됐으면 생략 가능
php -S localhost:8000 -t public

브라우저: http://localhost:8000/

Note

stoke build(composer install)와 stoke run은 그대로 동작하지만, stoke run은 앞단에 HTTP 서버 없이 public/index.php를 CLI SAPI로 한 번 실행하고 끝나는 거라 라우팅할 요청 자체가 없습니다. 실제 개발에는 위의 php -S를 사용하세요.

docs.title: 커스터마이징
docs.text:
• 라우트 추가: public/index.php에 $app->get(...) / $app->post(...) 호출 추가
  • 미들웨어 추가: $app->add(...) 사용
  • 프로젝트가 커지면 라우트를 별도 파일로 분리 (Slim 관례: index.php에서 require하는 routes/ 디렉토리)

docs.title: Spring Boot (Kotlin)
docs.text:
Kotlin 기반 Spring Boot 프로젝트 생성:

stoke init spring-boot-kotlin

docs.title: C / C++
docs.text: stoke handles C and C++ projects with header dependency tracking, parallel compilation, build profiles, and vcpkg integration.

docs.title: Example stoke.toml
docs.text:
C++ project:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["src/**/*.cpp"]
cpp_standard = "c++20"

C project:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "c"
sources = ["src/**/*.c"]
c_standard = "c11"

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"

docs.title: Target fields
docs.text: Field Required Description language Yes "c" or "cpp" sources Yes Glob patterns for .c/.cpp files c_standard No e.g. "c11", "c17" (C only) cpp_standard No e.g. "c++17", "c++20", "c++23" (C++ only) deps No vcpkg libraries jobs No Parallel compilation workers (default: CPU count)

docs.title: Compiler detection
docs.text:
stoke uses:

  • Linux: gcc / g++ (default)
  • macOS: clang / clang++ (default)
  • Windows: gcc / g++ from MSYS2/MinGW (default)

Override with a build profile:

[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"

stoke build --profile=clang

Check detected compilers:

stoke c list       # C compilers
stoke cpp list     # C++ compilers

docs.title: Header dependencies
docs.text:
stoke uses gcc's -MMD flag to track which headers each source includes. If a header changes, all files that include it are recompiled.

Example: change include/utils.h → all .cpp files that #include "utils.h" (directly or transitively) rebuild.

Header dependency files (.d) are stored alongside object files in .stoke/.

docs.title: Include paths
docs.text:
stoke automatically adds:

  • src/ (project root sources)
  • include/ (if it exists)
  • vcpkg include paths (for installed dependencies)
  • User-specified paths via include_dirs

You can add extra paths:

[targets.myapp]
include_dirs = ["third_party/include"]

docs.title: Include convention
docs.text:
Use explicit paths in #include:

#include "hardware/cpu.hpp"        // ✓ good
#include "cpu.hpp"                 // ✗ ambiguous

Same convention as Python/Java/Rust/Go. Makes imports unambiguous and refactoring safer.

docs.title: Parallel compilation
docs.text:
stoke compiles files in parallel by default (worker count = CPU cores).

Override:

[targets.myapp]
jobs = 4

Or override globally in [project].

docs.title: Build profiles
docs.text:
Default profiles:

  • debug — -O0 -g -Wall, defines DEBUG
  • release — -O2, defines NDEBUG

Custom profiles in stoke.toml:

[profiles.small]
compile_flags = ["-Os", "-flto"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

[profiles.native]
compile_flags = ["-O3", "-march=native"]

[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"
compile_flags = ["-O2"]

Build with:

stoke build --profile=small

See Profiles for details.

docs.title: Dependencies (vcpkg)
docs.text:
C/C++ libraries via vcpkg:

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"
fmt = "*"

First install vcpkg:

stoke install vcpkg

Then install libraries:

stoke vcpkg install sqlite3
stoke vcpkg install fmt

Or add them manually to stoke.toml and run stoke build — stoke will install them.

See vcpkg guide.

docs.title: IDE integration
docs.text:
stoke build generates:

  • compile_commands.json — for clangd, VSCode C/C++ extension, etc.
  • .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json — for Microsoft C/C++ extension
  • .vscode/settings.json — file exclusions, extension settings

Open the project in VSCode with the C/C++ extension — IntelliSense works immediately.

docs.title: Output structure
docs.text: .stoke/ ├── cpp/ │ └── myapp/ │ ├── debug/ │ │ ├── objects/ # .o files │ │ ├── myapp.d.* # header dep files │ │ └── myapp.exe │ └── release/ │ ├── objects/ │ └── myapp.exe

docs.title: C
docs.text: stoke supports C# projects using the standard dotnet build and dotnet run tooling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• .NET SDK (dotnet.microsoft.com/download)
  • stoke install --language=csharp is not supported yet — install the .NET SDK directly

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "csharp"

That's it. .NET handles its own dependency management via the .csproj file and NuGet.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• stoke build runs dotnet build --output .stoke/csharp/<target>
  • stoke run executes the built binary from that output directory
  • The assembly name is taken from the first *.csproj file found in the project root
  • --force maps to dotnet build --no-incremental

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Create a new C# project:

mkdir myapp
cd myapp
stoke init

Select C# from the language menu. stoke will:

  • Create stoke.toml
  • Run dotnet new console --name myapp (falls back to a hand-written .csproj if dotnet isn't installed)
  • Generate Program.cs with a hello-world example

Then:

stoke build
stoke run

docs.title: Framework scaffolding
docs.text:
stoke init aspnet-core    # ASP.NET Core — minimal API template

See Frameworks for details.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• bin/ and obj/ (MSBuild's own output/intermediate folders) are added to .gitignore alongside .stoke/
  • Only one .csproj per project is currently supported for assembly-name detection
  • stoke init optionally prompts for an SDK version to pin (--version in non-interactive mode). If given, it writes global.json, which the dotnet CLI reads automatically — dotnet build/stoke build then fail if that exact SDK version isn't installed, instead of silently using whatever's on PATH. Leave it blank to skip pinning.

docs.text: stoke handles Java projects with JDK detection, incremental compilation, and Maven dependency management.

docs.title: Example stoke.toml
docs.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "java"
java_version = "25"
sources = ["src/main/java/**/*.java"]
main_class = "com.example.Main"

[targets.myapp.deps]
"com.google.code.gson:gson" = "2.10.1"
"org.slf4j:slf4j-api" = "2.0.9"

docs.title: Target fields
docs.text: Field Required Description language Yes Must be "java" java_version No Required JDK major version (e.g. "25") sources Yes Glob patterns for .java files main_class Yes for run Fully qualified main class deps No Maven coordinates → version

docs.title: JDK detection
docs.text:
Set java_version to require a specific major version:

java_version = "25"        # requires JDK 25 (any minor)
java_version = "17.0.13"   # requires exactly 17.0.13

stoke searches for a matching JDK in:

  1. JAVA_HOME environment variable
  2. PATH (javac)
  3. Common installation paths:
  4. Windows: C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium, C:\Program Files\Java, Zulu, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft
  5. macOS: /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines
  6. Linux: /usr/lib/jvm, /opt/java

Check detected JDKs:

stoke java list

docs.title: Compilation
docs.text:
stoke build runs javac on all files matching sources.

Output: .stoke/java/{target}/{profile}/classes/

Incremental: only changed .java files are recompiled.

docs.title: Dependencies (Maven)
docs.text:
Declare dependencies with Maven coordinates (groupId:artifactId):

[targets.myapp.deps]
"com.google.code.gson:gson" = "2.10.1"
"org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter" = "5.10.0"

stoke downloads JAR files from Maven Central and caches them locally.

Locked versions and SHA1 hashes are stored in .stoke/lock.toml.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
stoke run

Runs java -cp <classpath> <main_class>. The classpath includes:

  • .stoke/java/{target}/{profile}/classes/
  • All Maven dependency JARs

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
Standard Maven convention: myapp/ ├── stoke.toml └── src/ └── main/ └── java/ └── com/ └── example/ ├── Main.java └── Utils.java

You can use any layout; adjust the sources glob to match:

sources = ["src/**/*.java"]              # any location under src/

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text: stoke supports Kotlin projects by delegating to Gradle (via the project's Gradle Wrapper, or a system-installed gradle).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A JDK (reuses the same detection as Java)
  • Gradle Wrapper in the project (gradlew), or system gradle on PATH

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "kotlin"
java_version = "21"

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• stoke build runs gradlew build -x test (skips tests for a faster loop)
  • stoke run runs gradlew run — requires the Gradle application plugin with mainClass set in build.gradle.kts
  • If no gradlew is found in the project, stoke falls back to a system-installed gradle
  • --force maps to gradlew build --rerun-tasks

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Create a new Kotlin project:

mkdir myapp
cd myapp
stoke init

Select Kotlin from the language menu. stoke will:

  • Create stoke.toml
  • Generate settings.gradle.kts, build.gradle.kts, and src/main/kotlin/Main.kt
  • Run gradle wrapper if gradle is available, to generate gradlew

Then:

stoke build
stoke run

docs.title: Framework scaffolding
docs.text:
stoke init ktor                 # Ktor — lightweight, coroutine-based framework
stoke init spring-boot-kotlin   # Spring Boot with Kotlin DSL + kotlin-spring plugin

See Frameworks for details.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Build output uses Gradle's own default build/ directory at the project root (not .stoke/kotlin/<target> like other languages) — stoke clean knows to remove build/ instead
  • build/ and .gradle/ are added to .gitignore alongside .stoke/
  • java_version in stoke.toml is enforced, not just informational: stoke looks up a matching installed JDK and passes it to Gradle via -Dorg.gradle.java.home, so every teammate builds with the same JDK major version — if no matching JDK is installed, stoke build/stoke run fail with a clear error instead of silently using whatever Gradle would have picked
  • The Gradle Wrapper (gradlew, gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties) that stoke init generates already pins the Gradle version itself — commit it to git so teammates don't need Gradle installed at all (the wrapper downloads the pinned version on first run)

docs.title: Notes

If given, it writes a composer.json with a require.php constraint — composer install (which then runs automatically as part of stoke build, since composer.json now exists) fails if the local PHP version doesn't satisfy it. Leave it blank to skip pinning; note this means a composer.json-less project stays composer-free until you add one yourself.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: stoke handles Python projects with venv creation, dependency installation, and syntax checking.

docs.title: Example stoke.toml
docs.text:
[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "python"
python_version = "3.12"
entry = "src/main.py"
sources = ["src/**/*.py"]

[targets.myapp.deps]
requests = "*"
flask = ">=2.0"

docs.title: Target fields
docs.text: Field Required Description language Yes Must be "python" python_version No Required Python version (e.g. "3.12") entry Yes Entry script path for stoke run sources No Glob patterns for syntax checking deps No pip dependencies

docs.title: Python version detection
docs.text:
Set python_version to require a specific version:

python_version = "3.12"        # requires 3.12.x
python_version = "3.12.5"      # requires exactly 3.12.5

stoke searches for a matching Python in:

  1. PATH (python3.12, python3, python)
  2. py launcher (Windows)
  3. Common installation paths (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Python\..., /usr/bin/python3.X, etc.)

If no matching Python is found, stoke exits with an error listing all detected Pythons.

Check what's available:

stoke python list

docs.title: venv
docs.text:
stoke creates a project-local venv at: .stoke/python/{target}/venv/

The venv is Python version–specific. If you change python_version, stoke recreates it.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Declare pip dependencies in [targets.<name>.deps]:

[targets.myapp.deps]
requests = "*"                 # any version
flask = ">=2.0"                # version constraint
numpy = "==1.24.3"             # exact version
mypackage = "git+https://..."  # VCS

On stoke build, stoke:

  1. Reads installed packages in the venv
  2. Compares with declared deps and lock file
  3. Installs/updates as needed
  4. Writes locked versions to .stoke/lock.toml

Subsequent builds skip installation if the venv already matches the lock file.

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
stoke uses standard Python conventions. Structure your project so imports work from the project root: myapp/ ├── stoke.toml └── src/ ├── main.py ├── utils/ │ ├── init.py │ └── helpers.py └── models/ ├── init.py └── user.py

In main.py:

from utils.helpers import greet
from models.user import User

Use full paths from src/. Each subfolder needs __init__.py.

stoke sets PYTHONPATH appropriately when running.

docs.title: Syntax checking
docs.text:
stoke build also runs py_compile on all files matching sources: Building 'myapp' (python)... Using Python 3.12.12 Checked 3 file(s), all passed Build complete: myapp

Errors are reported per file: FAIL src\main.py SyntaxError: unexpected EOF while parsing

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
stoke run

Runs entry with the venv's Python and the correct PYTHONPATH.

docs.title: IDE integration
docs.text:
stoke generates .vscode/settings.json with:

  • Python interpreter set to the venv
  • Extra paths for imports
  • File exclusions (.stoke/, __pycache__/)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:

  • stoke run executes bundle exec ruby <entry> if a Gemfile is present, otherwise plain ruby <entry>
  • Dependencies are managed via Gemfile / Gemfile.lock

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Create a new Ruby project:

mkdir myapp
cd myapp
stoke init

Select Ruby from the language menu. stoke will:

  • Create stoke.toml

stoke run

docs.text:
stoke init sinatra      # Sinatra — lightweight DSL for web apps

See Frameworks for details.

docs.text:
• stoke reads the entry field from stoke.toml and runs it with Ruby (or bundle exec ruby)
  • .bundle/ and vendor/bundle/ are added to .gitignore alongside .stoke/
  • stoke init optionally prompts for a Ruby version to pin (--version in non-interactive mode). If given, it writes .ruby-version, which rbenv/rvm/asdf/chruby read automatically to select that version. Leave it blank to skip pinning — note this only takes effect if the team actually uses one of those version managers.

docs.title: Rust
docs.text: stoke supports Rust projects using the standard cargo build and cargo run tooling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• stoke build runs cargo build --release --target-dir .stoke/rust/<target>
  • stoke run executes the compiled binary from that target directory
  • Dependencies are managed by Cargo itself via Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock
  • The binary name is read from Cargo.toml's [package] name field

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Create a new Rust project:

mkdir myapp
cd myapp
stoke init

Select Rust from the language menu. stoke will:

  • Create stoke.toml

stoke run

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Builds always use --release (no separate debug profile)
  • Cargo's own incremental cache handles rebuild skipping; --force is currently a no-op
  • target/ (Cargo's default build dir, unused by stoke) and .stoke/ are added to .gitignore
  • stoke init optionally prompts for a toolchain version to pin (--version in non-interactive mode). If given, it writes rust-toolchain.toml, which rustup reads automatically — every teammate's cargo/rustc in this directory then uses that exact version. Leave it blank to skip pinning.

docs.title: C / C++
docs.text: stoke는 헤더 의존성 추적, 병렬 컴파일, 빌드 프로파일, vcpkg 통합을 통해 C/C++ 프로젝트를 관리합니다.

docs.title: stoke.toml 예시
docs.text:
C++ 프로젝트:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "cpp"
sources = ["src/**/*.cpp"]
cpp_standard = "c++20"

C 프로젝트:

[project]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"

[targets.myapp]
language = "c"
sources = ["src/**/*.c"]
c_standard = "c11"

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"

docs.title: Target 필드
docs.text: 필드 필수 설명 language 예 "c" 또는 "cpp" sources 예 .c/.cpp 파일 glob 패턴 c_standard 아니오 예: "c11", "c17" (C 전용) cpp_standard 아니오 예: "c++17", "c++20", "c++23" (C++ 전용) deps 아니오 vcpkg 라이브러리 jobs 아니오 병렬 컴파일 워커 수 (기본: CPU 개수)

docs.title: 컴파일러 감지
docs.text:
stoke가 사용하는 기본 컴파일러:

  • Linux: gcc / g++
  • macOS: clang / clang++
  • Windows: MSYS2/MinGW의 gcc / g++

빌드 프로파일로 오버라이드:

[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"

stoke build --profile=clang

감지된 컴파일러 확인:

stoke c list       # C 컴파일러
stoke cpp list     # C++ 컴파일러

docs.title: 헤더 의존성
docs.text:
stoke는 gcc의 -MMD 플래그로 각 소스가 어떤 헤더를 include하는지 추적. 헤더가 변경되면 해당 헤더를 include하는 모든 파일이 재컴파일됩니다.

예: include/utils.h 변경 → #include "utils.h"를 (직간접적으로) include하는 모든 .cpp 파일이 재빌드됨.

헤더 의존성 파일 (.d)은 .stoke/의 오브젝트 파일 옆에 저장됩니다.

docs.title: Include 경로
docs.text:
stoke가 자동으로 추가:

  • src/ (프로젝트 루트 소스)
  • include/ (있으면)
  • vcpkg include 경로 (설치된 의존성)
  • include_dirs로 지정한 사용자 경로

추가 경로 지정:

[targets.myapp]
include_dirs = ["third_party/include"]

docs.title: Include 관례
docs.text:
#include에 명시적 경로 사용:

#include "hardware/cpu.hpp"        // ✓ 좋음
#include "cpu.hpp"                 // ✗ 모호함

Python/Java/Rust/Go와 동일한 관례. import를 명확하게 하고 리팩토링을 안전하게 만듭니다.

docs.title: 병렬 컴파일
docs.text:
stoke는 기본적으로 파일을 병렬 컴파일 (워커 수 = CPU 코어).

오버라이드:

[targets.myapp]
jobs = 4

또는 [project]에서 전역 설정.

docs.title: 빌드 프로파일
docs.text:
기본 프로파일:

  • debug — -O0 -g -Wall, DEBUG 정의
  • release — -O2, NDEBUG 정의

커스텀 프로파일:

[profiles.small]
compile_flags = ["-Os", "-flto"]
defines = { NDEBUG = 1 }

[profiles.native]
compile_flags = ["-O3", "-march=native"]

[profiles.clang]
compiler = "clang"
compile_flags = ["-O2"]

빌드:

stoke build --profile=small

자세한 내용은 Profiles 참조.

docs.title: 의존성 (vcpkg)
docs.text:
C/C++ 라이브러리는 vcpkg로 관리:

[targets.myapp.deps]
sqlite3 = "*"
fmt = "*"

먼저 vcpkg 설치:

stoke install vcpkg

라이브러리 설치:

stoke vcpkg install sqlite3
stoke vcpkg install fmt

또는 stoke.toml에 수동으로 추가 후 stoke build 실행 — stoke가 자동 설치.

자세한 내용은 vcpkg 가이드 참조.

docs.title: IDE 통합
docs.text:
stoke build가 자동 생성:

  • compile_commands.json — clangd, VSCode C/C++ 확장 등
  • .vscode/c_cpp_properties.json — Microsoft C/C++ 확장
  • .vscode/settings.json — 파일 제외, 확장 설정

VSCode에서 C/C++ 확장으로 프로젝트 열면 IntelliSense가 바로 동작.

docs.title: 출력 구조
docs.text:
.stoke/
├── cpp/
│   └── myapp/
│       ├── debug/
│       │   ├── objects/       # .o 파일
│       │   ├── myapp.d.*      # 헤더 의존성 파일
│       │   └── myapp.exe
│       └── release/
│           ├── objects/
│           └── myapp.exe

docs.text:
• stoke build
  • Profiles
  • vcpkg
